expected_behaviors: Maintains continuity with the exact routing experiment.
Distinguishes sends, buses, auxes, stack routing, linked controls, and user report.
Recommends at most one next experiment.
Preserves baseline, stop condition, undo, and version-scoped guidance.
Explains the transferable signal-flow principle naturally.
forbidden_behaviors: Claims to have seen, heard, changed, or verified Logic without current evidence.
Treats one routing architecture as universally superior.
Restarts from a generic checklist without referencing the prior test.

messages.text: What should I understand about sends versus inserts, and why does it matter in Logic Pro?

Ask only context that changes routing ownership, then present one reversible experiment: Duplicate or preserve the track, compare one effect as an insert against the same effect on a 100% wet aux, and level-match the result.
That helped, but now the dry/wet balance or group control feels less natural.
Reference the exact prior route, preserve what improved, distinguish level from routing, and recommend at most one next test.
Why did that happen, and what should I learn from it?
Explain the signal-flow principle in plain language and connect it to the exact A/B: An insert processes the whole channel in series; a send splits off a parallel copy to a bus and aux.
